Lifestyle itself is not directly measured by the supplied RegionLore data, but climate, housing, transportation, population change, and demographics provide useful context.

The clearest lifestyle distinction is climate. Austin is the warmest, with normal summer highs around 97–98°F and mild winters. Raleigh is cooler in summer and winter, while Denver has the coldest winters—normal January lows are about 18°F—and relatively low precipitation throughout the year. Raleigh is the wettest of the three, especially from June through September. These are 1991–2020 climate normals, so they describe long-term patterns rather than current-year conditions.

Housing costs favor Raleigh on the listed measures: its 2024 median rent was $1,572 and median home value $415,800, compared with $1,729 and $555,300 in Austin and $1,831 and $616,000 in Denver. Austin and Denver had higher median household incomes—$93,658 and $94,718 versus Raleigh’s $85,395—so the tradeoff is lower housing costs in Raleigh versus higher reported incomes in the other two cities.

The cities also differ in scale and growth. Austin is the largest, at about 1.0 million residents in 2025, while Denver had about 741,000 and Raleigh about 506,000. Raleigh grew fastest since 2020, at 8.6%, compared with Austin’s 4.2% and Denver’s 3.2%. Transportation patterns are broadly car-oriented in all three, with mean commutes close to 23–25 minutes. Denver stands out for higher transit and walking shares, while Austin has the highest work-from-home share.

Reported 2024 city crime rates also differ, though they should be interpreted as city-level law-enforcement data rather than a complete measure of day-to-day experience. Denver’s violent- and property-crime rates were higher than Austin’s and Raleigh’s; Raleigh’s violent-crime rate was slightly higher than Austin’s, while Austin’s property-crime rate was higher than Raleigh’s.

Overall, Raleigh offers the lowest listed housing costs and fastest recent growth, with a moderate climate. Austin offers the warmest weather, the largest population, and the highest work-from-home share, but higher housing costs. Denver combines the highest income and housing costs with colder, drier weather and somewhat more non-driving transportation—but also the highest reported crime rates among the three.
